Just realized that some of the methods now take locks on stores in differing orders, which can lead to deadlocks if one process calls `Exists()` while another calls, say `SetNames()`.  We've generally been taking the lock on the layers store, if it's being taken, before the lock for the images store, if it's being taken, and then the lock on the containers store, if it's being taken.
`CreateImage()` takes the images store lock before the layers store lock.
`CreateContainer()` takes the images lock, then the layers lock, then the containers lock.
`Exists()` takes the containers lock, then the images lock, then the layers lock.
`Mount()` and `Unmount()` take the containers lock, then the layers lock.
Those'll need to change the order in which they're acquiring locks in order to avoid creating deadlocks.

I'm really having trouble with changing the established behavior of `GetLockfile()`.  I'd like to try coming at it from another direction that looks roughly like:

* Add the parts of this PR that add read-only locks as a different type.  Basically, the `lockfile.go` bits, but renaming `RWLock()` to something starting with `Is`, a la `time.IsZero()`, so it doesn't keep confusing me into thinking it's some variation on the `Lock()` and `RLock()` methods of the `sync` package's mutex types.  
* Break out the methods of `LayerStore` and `ImageStore` that don't modify and try to `Save()` their contents out into separate read-only interfaces (`ROLayerStore` or something), and modify the existing interfaces to embed the read-only interfaces rather than listing each of the same methods.  This would also be done to `FileBasedStore`, `MetadataStore`, `BigDataStore`, and `FlaggableStore`.
* Add new variants of `newLayerStore` and `newImageStore` that obtain read-only locks instead of read-write locks, use them to create underlying objects of the same `layerStore` and `imageStore` types that the current functions do, and return the objects using the read-only interface types.
* Switch to using the read-only interface types for handling additional read-only layer and image stores in the main `Store` object.  The writable stores should mix right in when we're building slices of stores.

This should let us use build-time type-checking to avoid inadvertently calling code paths that try to modify things, letting them change in-memory contents as they do, and then failing to `Save()` them to disk.  As you've noted out of band, reverting the in-memory changes when that happens is still something we need to handle, but this should help us avoid inflicting that on ourselves.

What do you think?

Whiteouts are entries in a layer tar archive which are used to indicate that items, presumably added in previous layers, should be removed when applying the layer's contents to a directory tree as part of the iterative process of creating a root filesystem for a container.  The conventions used in layer tar archives are modeled after the ones used by aufs.

When generating change lists or diffs, the current logic generates whiteout for a directory (indicated, in the style of aufs, by placing a file named `..wh..wh..opq` in the directory) if the `trusted.overlay.opaque` extended attribute on the directory as set to `y`.  Now that this extended attribute is set more often, an archive that adds a new subdirectory, which should contain entries for the parent directory and the new subdirectory, now also includes a whiteout entry.

For example, building an image named "foo" using the Dockerfile 
```
FROM alpine
RUN mkdir /root/subdirectory && touch /root/subdirectory/regularfile
```
and then using `skopeo copy` to copy its layers to a temporary subdirectory using `skopeo copy docker-daemon:foo:latest dir:/path/to/subdir`, and then using `tar tf` to list the contents of the archive, should produce
```
root/
root/subdirectory/
root/subdirectory/regularfile
```

Instead, we get
```
root/
root/subdirectory/
root/subdirectory/.wh..wh..opq
root/subdirectory/regularfile
```

When applying that layer, the `.wh..wh..opq` is treated as an instruction to delete the directory, which is incorrect.  If the directory has contents, it will be recreated automatically (which makes this hard to spot in the wild), but not necessarily with the same permissions.  If the directory doesn't have contents, it's just deleted.

A different but similar code path is used for `docker diff`, and can be observed by running `docker run --name foo alpine sh -c 'mkdir /root/subdirectory && touch /root/subdirectory/regularfile'` and using `docker diff foo` to list the changes (**C**hanges, **A**dditions, **D**eletions) made to the container.  Instead of
```
C /root
A /root/subdirectory
A /root/subdirectory/regularfile
```
we get
```
C /root
D /root/subdirectory
A /root/subdirectory/regularfile
```

I'm revising this patch to check for the presence of similarly-named items in lower layers when deciding whether or not to consider an opaque directory as having been removed and recreated, rather than as simply having been created.

The output of the overlay driver's "changes" logic (which backends "docker diff") is not used by the overlay driver's "diff" logic (which is used to produce layer diffs), but they both get tripped up by the way the opaque attribute is used and produce different results than other storage drivers do.

This incorrect handling of the opaque attribute breaks things if the directory which is marked as opaque either has no content (in which case we produce a layer that includes only opaque whiteout for that directory, and extracting that layer doesn't create the directory, even though it should exist) or needs permissions or ownership other than an unspecified default (since the directory will be created so that its contents can be put down on the filesystem, but the correct permission and ownership information will have been lost).  If, for example, such a directory needs ownership and permissions set on it so that a process running as a non-root user in the container can access the directory's contents, that's a critical problem.

The added logic for catching this case is all but certain to slow down a build, but keep in mind that the baseline for comparison is still NaiveDiff.

The layer diffs themselves don't include opaqueness encoded as an extended attribute, since they use aufs-style formats for representing whiteout information.  Opaque directories are marked as such by including a "file" named `.wh..opq.` under the corresponding directory in the archive, along with the directory itself.  On extraction, the presence of the `.wh..opq.` entry in a directory is interpreted as an instruction to add the `trusted.overlay.opaque`=`y` attribute to the directory.  Because this change is directly applied to the `diff` tree as part of extracting it, rather than being applied to a directory on a mounted overlay filesystem, the new kernel-side optimization is not, and would not have been, triggered when extracting downloaded layers.

The main thing I'd want to be sure of is that we're handling whiteout information correctly, since overlay uses device nodes for whiteout, and extended attributes to mark opacity.  Specifically, I'd want to be sure that if an image creates files or directories in one layer, then removes them in a second layer that is applied on top of that first layer, that we're not losing that information when we extract the image into local storage.  Likewise, if a directory is marked as opaque, that the commit/checkout step doesn't discard that information.

One way to verify this would be to find a multi-layered image whose history shows it creating files in one layer, then using "rm" to remove those files in a different layer, creating whiteout information in that layer, or an image where a directory was marked as opaque, signifying that it had been removed and then recreated within a single layer.  (That an image does this could be verified for certain by copying the image to a "dir:" location with skopeo, and examining the layer blobs directly using "tar tvf".  Whiteout entries for files and directories will have `.wh.` prefixed to their basenames, and opaque directories contain a `.wh..opq.` "file".)

For example, `docker.io/ubuntu@sha256:d3fdf5b1f8e8a155c17d5786280af1f5a04c10e95145a515279cf17abdf0191f` contains a layer with blobsum `3009ec50c8871f7a3f19c248194270a1a3aa28705934d619acbd96c663ce5c89` which removes the files in `/var/lib/apt/lists/`, while `docker.io/redis@sha256:26c93c5b06eaa323bb1089500f42b0dd158138772348b865e364127f1d554982` contains a layer with blobsum `67b22db27e5144c14efdf55d9cef9c3dadffb43593790ec99663fb1b783dbb6b` which marks `/var/lib/apt/lists/partial` as opaque.

The root filesystem of a working container created by versions of buildah built with and without the patch, if both versions are forced to download the image, should have the same set of files, with the same contents.  In particular, deleted files for which whiteout exists in the image's blobs, and the contents of directories from layers before they were marked as opaque, should not be present in the container.
